newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: FOCUS-Japan against double standards on environment.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Japan against double standards on environment.

text.p: Japan, pushing for legal whale-hunting and backing a controversial proposal to end a world ban in ivory trading, urged the world community on Monday not to employ double standards on environmental issues.

Nobutoshi Akao, Japan's ambassador to the Geneva-based Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), told a 10-day CITES conference that decisions on conservation of wildlife resources should be based on universal principles.
The Zimbabwe meeting will consider nearly 80 proposals on endangered species, with the ones on ivory trade and whale hunting at the top.

"Our decisions on these important issues must not be based on emotion, but on credible scientific findings, on the respect for culture and traditions and on the recognition of the different values guiding the world," Akao said.

"We must avoid double standards in our approach. It has become all the more important for us to address challenges confronting us in a new, innovative and creative way," he said, adding that there was no single philosophy to conservation and that final responsibility lay with individual governments.

Akao's comments dovetailed with a speech by Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe who opened the meeting by urging the international community to reward sustainable wildlife management or face certain environmental disaster.
Mugabe said countries should not be deprived access to their natural wealth.
Elephant-rich Zimbabwe, Namibia, and Botswana are sponsoring a proposal at the CITES conference for a partial lifting of a seven-year-old ban on ivory sales.

The three countries and their supporters, notably Japan, say they must be allowed some limited but strictly supervised trade because their elephant herd, now estimated at around 150,000, is rising steadily and was doing so even before the 1989 ban.

Since the ban was imposed they have accumulated nearly 100 tonnes of ivory from annual culls and from legally hunted trophies. They say trade in ivory is vital to stabilise the elephant herd, which they say is now over twice the land's carrying capacity.

"There must be encouragement of sustainable utilisation and development for those whose policies and actions uphold scientifically accepted standards, while penalising those that abuse the environment," Mugabe said to applause mainly from the Zimbabwean contingent among the more than 2,000 delegates and observers at the CITES meeting.
Mugabe said wildlife in Southern Africa was mostly found in arid and semi-desert regions where water was expensive to pump.
"Elephants, especially because of their huge bodies, consume large amounts of this underground water and, we believe, every species must pay its way to survival," he said.

The proposal to allow ivory sales is strongly opposed by some influential green movements and countries, including the U.S.-based African Elephant Foundation, and the United States and French governments. They argue lifting the ban will leave elephants at the mercy of poachers.
The 138-member CITES will vote on the issue towards the end of the 10-day conference.
